sections.title: Prerequisite: From Discrete to Continuous
sections.content: Briefly recap discrete probability (histograms with bars). Explain that when we measure continuous data (e.g., exact height or weight), the probability of any single point is zero, necessitating a 'density' approach.
sections.example: A histogram of student heights starts as bars; as we increase the number of students, the bars become thinner, eventually forming a smooth 'bell curve' shape.

sections.title: Defining the PDF Curve
sections.content: Introduce the PDF: f(x) represents the 'density' of probability. Emphasize the two golden rules: 1. f(x) ≥ 0, and 2. The total area under the curve must equal 1.
sections.example: Visualize a 'Probability Fluid' being poured onto a graph. The total amount of fluid is exactly 1 liter, spread out over the horizontal axis.

sections.title: Calculating Probability as Area
sections.content: Demonstrate that the probability of a range [a, b] is the definite integral of the PDF over that range. Visually represent this as the shaded area under the curve between two vertical lines.
sections.example: A delivery drone’s arrival time follows a PDF. The probability that it arrives between 2:00 PM and 2:10 PM is the 'shaded area' under the curve between those two time marks.

sections.title: Real-world Application: The Reliable Robot
sections.content: Consolidate learning by applying the concept to a practical scenario. Show how the peak of the curve represents the most likely range (the mode).
sections.example: A robot arm’s precision in picking up an apple: The PDF shows the highest 'density' at the exact center of the apple, with the total area proving that the robot will eventually touch the apple somewhere within its reach.

sections.title: Conclusion & Key Takeaways
sections.content: Summarize that PDF is not probability itself, but the 'density' of probability. Remind students that the curve tells us where outcomes cluster.
sections.example: A quick visual recap: A 'tall' peak means outcomes are highly clustered; a 'flat' curve means outcomes are widely spread out.
